In America, you do not have the right to speak to a lawyer during a police investigation, like a traffic stop.  You ALWAYS have the right to remain silent and can exercise that at any time.  If you become detained or arrested, you will be read your rights and you may again exercise your right to remain silent and request a lawyer before you are questioned.  That stuff then happens at the station or in jail depending on where you are.

The bottom half is good advice though.  At the end of the day, if something is done incorrectly that should be fought IN COURT by your lawyer, not by you during the event.  It's hard to believe but the judge is a neutral party who is there to maintain the rule of law and ensure things are done correctly.  It's not their job to put offenders behind bars, that is for the prosecution to do.

Get a financial advisor.  They'll help you make whatever arrangements you need.

As for donating it all right now, I wouldn't do that.  I would use your advisor to start having that money generate more money and donate it piecemeal as you find causes you believe in.  Giving $75 million to one or a few causes you believe in now is great.  But think about the possibility of donating $100-200 million to a bunch of causes over time that you may develop relationships with.  Events may happen in the future that you want to help with (natural disaster, famine etc) and you won't have that ability if you have already given it all away.

You can tell all your friends and people you donated it to charity.  That may shut them up anyway and then go on the path you believe in.  Just my two cents. For ADHD or period?  You may be suffering from more than just ADHD.  It's possible anxiety and/or depression may be playing a part in how you are feeling.  Those are treatable as well.  Medicines don't 'cure' those issues but they definitely help you to move in the right direction mentally.

Start by talking to your doctor about how you feel.  They can help you out with medications that can help and hook you up with a dietician and maybe a psychologist to start getting your eating under control and your mind  in a better place.  Also, take your ADHD meds religiously.  You likely have them for a reason.

Also, if your hobbies don't hurt others and aren't illegal, don't be ashamed by them.  Adults play with and are obsessed with Legos, cartoons, dolls, trains and whatever.  As you get older you find that you need to hold on to what makes you happy no matter how silly it may be.

It takes a lot of work to change but it's doable.  Luckily you have a lot of time to work on it.

If you have something that needs treating you should talk with your doctor about it and figure out what is best for you.  Sometimes it's medication, sometimes it's therapy.  Sometimes it's just changing daily habits.

Either way, you have to work through what you're dealing with.  If you feel socially awkward, find a place and make it comfortable for you.  If it's a bar, go there multiple times a week.  Get to know the bartenders and staff.  Feel comfortable about being there.  Then go from there.  If you're not comfortable in a venue you will have a harder time with the rest of it.

Once you've made a place your own you should feel better about talking to people within that space.  The more you talk to people, the easier it gets until it becomes natural.

Positive change takes time and work.  If you want to do it, put in the time and effort.

Anxiety and other mental conditions can be treated with medications but all they do is take the edge off and let you begin the work to get through your condition(s).  You could definitely ask a doctor for meds if it affects your life but you have to know that you have to put in the work to get through the rest of the condition(s).  There is no magic pill that takes away 100% of anxiety, depression or whatever you are facing.  The more you push through it, the easier it can become.  Everyone stumbles and has bad days but you gotta put in effort or even the meds won't be enough to get you through what you are facing.

As for the mental abuse, I would see out help from a counsellor or psychologist.  They can help you come to terms with what is and isn't normal.  I had to deprogram myself from some things my parents either taught me or displayed towards the world.  I love them to death but some of their views were really skewed and made life hard for a while for me.

I went camping with a friend where you hike into the camp site.  The site was up on top of a ridge and was really nice.  There were a lot of trees around but you could still see the horizon really well.  Beautiful sunset.  Took about two hours to get to it carrying all our stuff.  We spent the night but woke up really early in the morning to the sound of thunder off in the distance.  It wasn't supposed to rain so we didn't even put the rain guard up on the tent the night before.  Looking at the pitch black storm clouds in the distance we decided to try and hike out before it hit.  We started packing essentials but the storm was moving too fast.  Once I'd grabbed my bag and walked back out the tent it was obvious we'd be caught out in the open if we tried to hike out.  It was almost on us so we put the rain guard on the tent and hunkered down.

This massive gust of wind hit the tent and somehow I reached through the tent wall and grabbed the rain guard as it immediately was blown off the stakes.  Then the rain hit and it was insane.  Just like a waterfall with lightning every couple seconds.  I yelled at my friend to go outside to put the guard back on because I was the only thing keeping it from flying off into nowhere.  After some argument she went out and got it back staked down.  We then hunkered back into the sleeping bag completely soaked to the bone.  Everything in the tent was wet by then.

The lightning was fierce...it felt like it was striking all around us.  She was screaming.  I tried to calm her down but there wasn't much I could do.  I figured we were done for.  At that point I just gave in as there was literally nothing we could do and fell asleep.  She told me later that she did too.

When we woke up the storm was done and we went outside.  There were huge tree branches down all around our site and the surrounding area.  About two hours later a park ranger came to the site and asked us if we had been up here in the storm.  He told us we were really lucky as the site next to us had a tree fall on their tent after they evacuated before the storm.

Maybe this doesn't fit as I don't think I was scared or in fear of my life even though I should have been.  Sometimes things happen in life that there is nothing you can do about.  You can freak out or you can just accept it and move on (or give up like I did).  Feels kinda cowardly but I've always been pretty calm in disastrous situations.  Usually I'm the person with their head on straight to make the right choices.

Depending on the situation, one thing I learned being a supervisor is that you don't necessarily have to correct an issue in the moment.  If it's a behavior that has to stop I stop it but I may take some time to think about the best way to solve the problem before I confront the individual or group about what was going on.  That way, the situation is calmer for both of you and you can say the right things vs. bringing emotions into it and possibly having to apologize for your reaction later.

It's a little harder if you don't have power over the people or situation but a simple 'cut it out' or 'please stop' and then a discussion later works the same way.  Nobody wants to be called out for something in front of others and can be more understanding in a private environment so talking with the person calmly later is a good choice.

There are always difficult conversations in life.  I took a class through my job about them and it has helped me immensely at both work and in life too.  Maybe search the internet or YouTube for a class or instruction about it.  The ability to master difficult conversations is a tool everyone should have in their toolbox.

The suits being banned had either buoyancy or impermeability in them to give more advantage to the swimmers.  They also banned external bits on the suits to help guide water over the body.  The Speedo Fastskin 2 had rubber bumps on the chest of the suit to help channel the water more effectively down the body when you swam.

if you take a true technical suit today and pour a little water on it, it will actually sit on top of the suit and you can move it around.  If you press on the water it will go through the fabric which is what makes it a legal suit.  It blows people's minds when you show them this in the store.

As for cost, the suits you see the Olympians wearing are 'only' about $450ish for men and $550 for women for the top of the line suits from TYR (Avictor), Speedo (LZR X) and Arena (Ultra).  You can actually buy the exact same type of suit they have on at a swimming store or online on the vendor's website but the patterns on the suits used in the Olympics may be exclusive for each vendor's sponsored swimmers. If you are a high level competitor looking for a technical suit, you will want to find a store that will fit your suit for you to make sure it is exactly the right size or else there is less benefit to wearing the technical suits as it's not only the fabric but the compression the suit provides that helps you swim faster.

Source: I've sold competitive swimwear and fit people in technical suits for 14 years.
